one_liner: Plain C async printf-style logger; producer-side calls about 3.5x faster than spdlog when buffers are not full.
what_it_does: haclog is an asynchronous logging library in C11 with a printf-style macro API (HACLOG_INFO, HACLOG_DEBUG, and so on), console, file, size-rotating and time-rotating handlers, and a customizable meta prefix. You add handlers, start one detached backend thread with haclog_backend_run(), and call haclog_thread_context_init() and haclog_thread_context_cleanup() in each logging thread. It is not a drop-in for spdlog: the API is C macros with printf format strings, not fmt-style C++ calls.
how_it_is_fast: Each producer thread owns a single-producer/single-consumer byte ring buffer (default 1 MiB, minimum 1 MiB) and writes only a header, the raw binary arguments and copies of %s strings into it; formatting is deferred to the backend thread. The format string is parsed once per call site into a cached 'printf primitive' (static pointer guarded by a spinlock on first use), so the hot path is a timestamp, a switch over the precomputed argument types and memcpy. The backend thread polls every thread's buffer, formats with its own vsprintf reimplementation, and sleeps 100 ns when idle.
when_to_use: C or mixed C/C++ code bases that want an async logger without a C++ dependency
Bursty logging where the per-thread buffer rarely fills, so the producer only pays the enqueue cost (about 148 ns per call in the author's run, vs 518 ns for spdlog async)
Latency-sensitive threads that must not lose log lines: a full buffer blocks the producer instead of dropping
Applications needing printf-style formatting with plain-text output readable by tail (unlike PlatformLab NanoLog's binary log)
when_not_to_use: Sustained high-rate logging: in the same benchmark's min-time scenario (buffers full) haclog takes 1590 ns per call at 1 thread vs spdlog async 606 ns and spdlog sync 556 ns, and 2684 ns vs 1872 and 1235 ns at 8 threads (derived from page data), so it is slower than spdlog once the buffer fills
When you want the fastest async logger available: in the same shootout NanoLog (60 ns at 1 thread in scenario 2, 161 ns in scenario 1) and Quill bounded dropping (52 ns in scenario 1) beat it
Code that builds format strings at run time: the format must be a string literal, enforced only in C++ builds
Many short-lived threads: each thread allocates its own ring buffer (1 MiB minimum, 4 MiB in the benchmark) and cleanup polls in 1 ms sleeps until the backend drains it
Programs that need a clean shutdown of the logger: the backend thread is detached and loops forever with no stop API

integration.form: shared lib (default BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON) or static lib; CMake and Meson builds
integration.dependencies: none (Google Benchmark and a test library are downloaded only when benchmarks or tests are enabled)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (CMake sets C and C++ standard 11); CMake 3.18.6+ or Meson
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows (MSVC), macOS, Android per CI badges; x86-64 benchmarked only
integration.thread_safety: Logging from many threads is supported via per-thread SPSC buffers; each thread must init/clean up its context (auto-init on first log is on by default). Adding handlers is not synchronized and should happen before haclog_backend_run().

gotchas: A message larger than half the per-thread buffer minus 128 bytes fails haclog_bytes_buffer_w_fc and the serializer calls haclog_debug_break() and returns, so the line is dropped (and a debug build traps).

Memory ordering is thin: the reader publishes its position with a relaxed store and producers read it relaxed, and the per-call-site primitive pointer uses double-checked locking on a plain (non-atomic) static; fine on x86's strong ordering, but formally a data race and worth auditing before use on ARM.
With more than 128 %s arguments in one message the serializer substitutes '(haclog str cache full)' without consuming the va_arg, which shifts the remaining arguments.
The README's hello sample calls haclog_thread_context_init() a second time where it means haclog_thread_context_cleanup(); the benchmark used tag v0.4.0 while the repo is at 0.4.5.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick haclog over fmtlog, Quill or BinLog when the project must stay plain C or wants printf-style calls without a C++ toolchain dependency; if C++ is fine, the same author's benchmark shows NanoLog, Quill and fmtlog as fast or faster, especially under sustained load.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's public cc_log_benchmark (Google Benchmark, 2000 iterations x 5 repetitions, struct of four integers plus a 128-char string with full metadata pattern, file output, 4 MiB per-thread buffer, GCC 14.2.1 Release, i7-10710U fixed at 3.2 GHz), haclog v0.4.0 measured 148 ns median per call at 1 thread vs spdlog v1.12.0 async 518 ns and sync 587 ns. That run never fills the buffer; in the same report's sustained min-time scenario haclog is 2-3x slower than spdlog at 1, 2 and 8 threads and only ahead at 4 threads (1495 vs 1752 ns async).
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-08, version 0.4.5, 82 stars, no open issues), MIT-licensed, small (about 30 source files) and easy to vendor, but a one-author project with first-party benchmarks only.
